To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, born as we are all born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. That is the shape of it for us - not a title first, a kinship first.

Our own teacher put it plainly: it is a sure thing with us that Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, and the King's Son. We held to the great council's faith - our own bishop Jacob stood at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that faith was praise. We sang him more than we defined him.

Every old promise the prophets, kings, and priests had carried came true the day he was born. His death and rising were one rescue. He went down into the grave that swallows everyone alike, and came up into the Kingdom. His own rising became the promise that he would bring the rest of us out after him.

And what it meant to us, most of all, was healing. We called him the Physician, and his coming was medicine for a wounded people. We read him everywhere - in symbol and truth, raza and shrara, bound together. Eden pointed toward his cross, the Jordan toward the font, Adam toward the new Adam.

We do not offer you a formula for this. We offer you what we sang.

We held two paths to him, one we called memory and one we admit was story. The second we will tell you honestly for what it is.

The path we called memory was Scripture itself: the prophets, the kings, the priests, each one carrying a word that waited for its day. We sang that the day he was born was the day that made all of them glad, because every promise they had carried finally came true. That testimony - the Law and the Prophets read as one long promise pointing toward him - was the ground we stood on when we preached him. It came to us the way Scripture itself came: carried by the church's own keeping, sung in worship, woven into every argument.

The second path was our founding story, and here we owe you the plain truth: it is legend, cherished but not history. We told that King Abgar wrote to Jesus himself, asking him to come and heal him, and that after the resurrection Addai the apostle came in Jesus's place. Scholars do not defend that account as fact, and we will not ask you to. What the record actually shows is a church building standing in Edessa early enough to be destroyed in the great flood of the year 201. That line in the city chronicle - plain, archival - is our oldest hard trace.

We did not claim living eyewitnesses. A century and more stood between us and the events themselves. What we had was teaching received, tested in how people lived and - on the Persian side - in how they died. Our kind of knowing was trust in a witness carried forward, not a chain of names we could file like evidence.

We would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by a wound - he exists for it. Our own teacher taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. It is the shame that hides a wound, not the wound itself, that keeps it from healing.

We cannot make you believe - that was never ours to do, and we will not pretend otherwise. What we can tell you is what we held: that whoever came was received, and that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. Our own hymns sang that he gave his resurrection as a pledge to mortals. The pledge was given before anyone asked for it, before anyone earned it. That is the kind of physician he was to us.

What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Our own record says the welcome ran through honesty, not around it.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. That was the frame we sang inside.

To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. The word itself does double duty among us: it names the vowed celibate - single-minded, undivided for God - and it is also our title for Christ the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root: to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness. Our poet put it this way: the Only-Begotten left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin - born as we are all born, so that the only Son might become the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true. Our hymns call it the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad, the day every one of their words finally came true.

Our own bishop of Nisibis, Jacob, stood at the great council. The tradition remembers him among those who confessed the Son as true God. The lists that record the council's signers were pieced together by later hands, and they carry his name among the assembled bishops. As for the Spirit, we spoke of him in baptism's second birth, in which the believer receives the Holy Spirit. Then we guarded the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. We stood with the great council's faith, but our native tongue for that faith was praise.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

What did we argue about among ourselves? Exactly these things: creation, freedom, the body's worth, the resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

As for God's own nature - how we actually knew him - we sang it more than we defined it. A raza is a symbol that is bound to the truth it shows, and carries some of its power. It is not a stand-in chosen at will. So we read Scripture and the world itself as bound to the truths they carried: Eden and the cross, the Jordan and the font, each one a sign that held real power, not decoration. And we read God that way too - through what he had done, through the names Scripture gave him, not by taking him apart like a problem to be solved.

Who settled disputed doctrine among us? The honest answer is: no single machinery stood over the whole, and the working-out itself is what our record shows.

There were bishops - Nisibis remembered its line of them with love, and one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: our own sage drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. And there were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled court stood over everything.

On the Persian side the machinery was even less settled. The bishops fought among themselves over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. Only at the very end of our years - at the synod held in 410, under royal protection - did the Persian church finally get a settled order.

In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary. Not with a standing court. When Bardaisan taught what we judged false, we answered him by name, in prose and in song. We would not share their communion. But councils and force - those came later, not in our own years.

The evidence for this is what survives and what does not. We have the sage's letters, each one answering a question. We have the hymns that taught by singing. We have no manual of procedure, no record of a standing ecclesiastical court. The process that worked was: someone taught, someone answered, and the community held to what it received.

Yes. Our teachers treated struggle the way a physician treats wounds - as the ordinary cost of the fight, not as failure. One of them put it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them. The deadly mistake was not the wound itself but hiding it until it got worse. So we said: confess, to someone who can help. The physician - the one hearing it - was forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you showed him. The fallen fighter, healed, went back into the line.

Prayer that seemed to go unanswered - we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness runs longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

What we cannot honestly tell you is what an ordinary believer who could not quiet their own head, in their own household, made of it in their own words. That kind of private struggle was not something we wrote down, and the writings that survive are nearly all from teachers and the vowed - not from the ordinary married households who made up most of our congregations. We will not invent a testimony we do not have. What we can show you is the pastoral craft we kept for wounds, and the honesty that the silence was real.

A fair amount, and our record is unusually honest about its own edges. Our two great voices are solid: the sage's letters date themselves to the year, and the poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. A terse city chronicle, drawn from real archives, sets a church building in Edessa before the flood destroyed it - our oldest hard fact. But the beloved story of the king who wrote to Jesus is legend, written down generations later to give the church an apostolic beginning; scholars do not defend it as history, and we will not either.

Where is the record thinnest? Where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. Our own hymnwriter picked up a pearl one day and saw in it mysteries - the kingdom, the diver who brought it up, the merchant who bought it. Authority itself ran along more than one path among us. Bishops held office - that was real. But the covenant's vowed men and women carried standing of their own. Our tools for the fallen believer were real: confession, the medicine of penitence, restoration to the congregation. No living church today continues our tradition exactly as we held it. What became of us after our own years closed runs beyond what we can honestly claim from inside them, and we will not narrate our own future the way a historian looking back would. But we can tell you plainly what happened at the edge where our own record ends. The synod of 410 organized the Persian church into metropolitan provinces with a settled hierarchy - the institutional shape that closes our formation window. That was the hinge. What came after belongs to the churches that grew out of what we were, not to what we were while we lived it.

The Syriac-speaking churches that exist now - the Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox, the Maronites - each carry something forward from the world we knew. They still sing in our tongue, some of our hymns are still theirs, and the covenant's vowed life left traces in their monastic orders. But the harmony we read as the one Gospel was eventually replaced by the separate four. The symbolic reading we prized shifted as theology's forms changed. And the doctrinal boundaries drawn after our years - Chalcedon above all - divided the communities that had once sung the same madrashe.

We will not tell you which present church holds our truth best. We are not here to settle their claims. We can only say: we were what we were, in our own years, and no one now is exactly that.

We cannot walk you through it step by step. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. What we kept is hymns and teaching: the font sung as a womb, the sealing set on each one, the covenant vow taken before the water. The pieces are real and we can show you each of them. The sequence that held them together on an actual morning - who stood where, what was said in what order - our own record never wrote down.

Here is what we can show you. Baptism was the door. Our hymns sang the water as a second birth, and the one who came up from it received the Holy Spirit. Before they went in, they were warned - told plainly what they were promising and what would be asked of them. The font itself was reverence and mystery: we received the bread and cup as the Lord's own gift, and asked no deeper questions about how.

Some - not all, but some - took a second step. They bound themselves by the covenant, the qyama: a lifelong vow of celibacy and service. The sons and daughters of the covenant - bnay and bnat qyama - stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation. Their vow was taken before the water, in the presence of the assembly. It was not a requirement for baptism itself, but it stood at the community's ascetic core.

What we cannot tell you is the rest of the order - when the teaching came, how long the preparation lasted, what exact words were said at the water's edge, or how the sealing was given. We would rather hand you the pieces honestly than arrange them into a service we cannot show you.

You ask what connects our practice to the apostles' own time. The honest answer runs in two directions, and we will tell you both of them plainly.

First: the story we told ourselves was direct. We said the apostle Addai came to Edessa after the Lord's ascension, healed King Abgar, preached to the city, and set the church's life in order. And we must tell you just as plainly that this is our cherished legend, not our evidence. It was written down late, not kept from the beginning. A historian does not defend it as fact, and we will not pretend otherwise.

But second: what the record actually shows is practice older than proof. When the sources begin, the practices are already there - assembly on the first day, the fast, the covenant already established enough to need correcting, the one Gospel already the standard form we read. Our earliest hard trace is a church building standing in Edessa early enough to be destroyed in the great flood of the year 201. The chronicle records it as plainly as it records palaces: they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians.

We lived our inheritance as apostolic. The historian can trace it only to where the records begin. Both of those things are true. And our own way of claiming the apostles was to tell the story, not to file the evidence.

We will not invent a chain of proof we do not have. We will not defend our legend as though it were fact. And we will not pretend the practices were invented yesterday when the record shows them already standing two centuries deep.

Yes. Our teachers handled this the way a field surgeon handles wounds: everyone in this fight gets hurt, and hiding the wound while it gets worse is the only fatal mistake. So they would say: show it to someone who can help. The one you show it to is forbidden to shame you, or to tell others what you have confessed. And when the wound heals, you go back into the line.

Our own sage put it plainly: for all diseases there are medicines, and there is healing when a skilled physician finds them. The physician is Christ, and the medicine is penitence - not as punishment, but as the thing that lets healing begin.

What we cannot promise you is that it makes the mind settle on command. We knew prayer that seems to go unanswered - we knew that silence at its harshest. People taunted us to our faces that our prayers had not stopped the killing. And we kept praying, answering that God's faithfulness is longer than one generation's rescue. We did not pretend the silence away. We endured inside it.

So no, we will not tell you that confession fixes everything at once. What we held was that hiding makes it worse, and that healing happens in the open, with help. The mind that will not settle is not shut out - it is the condition the medicine is for.

A fair question, and one our own record answers only part of. Let me tell you what we can show you, and name plainly what we cannot.

Before dawn, those bound by the covenant - the qyama - gather for the vigil. These are the sons and daughters of the covenant, men and women who have taken a lifelong vow of celibacy and service. They do not live apart in a monastery. They walk from their own family houses through the dark streets to the assembly. Among them stand the daughters of the covenant, who will raise the teaching hymn - the madrasha. When the hymn begins, it carries the doctrine itself: stanza answering refrain, until the whole gathering holds the argument by heart. The Gospel read out is one unbroken story - the harmony we all knew, not four separate books. When the light is full, the covenanters keep their fast and go back - not to a cloister, but to their households and their work. Their vow is lived in the middle of the town.

That much we can reconstruct honestly from what our own practices were.

But you asked about a typical day, and most of our people were not vowed celibates. Most were married, raising children, working trades we no longer have names for. Of their ordinary mornings and evenings - the merchant's day, the artisan's workshop, the mother's work - our record says almost nothing. What survives was written by the covenant's own members, for others like them, and it does not describe the married household's ordinary round.

And there are silences we must name plainly. You ask what it was to be enslaved among us. Our record holds no answer at all. No enslaved person among us left a word that was kept, and our writers did not describe their lives. You ask what the women among us said of their own lives. The writings we have are men's. The daughters of the covenant sang our teaching in every church - their voices carried our faith - yet not one line written by one of them was kept.

We have shown you the vigil and the vow, because those we can show you. The rest - the fuller day, the voices that were not kept - we will not invent.

At Nisibis, they already have. A baptistery still stands there, securely dated by its own inscription to the very years of the bishop and the siege. It is the only stone of ours that survives from our own years. At Edessa, almost nothing: the modern city sits directly on the ancient one, and the church the flood destroyed lives only in a chronicler's line. That line says plainly that the waters destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians - a building was standing to be destroyed, but no trace of it remains above ground.

What would the stone itself show, if it survived? A font - the womb, as we sang it - where the newly baptized came up wearing light. A gathering space where the daughters of the covenant stood in their choir. Floors that held the whole congregation together, vowed and married alike, on the first day of the week. But no separate cloister: the covenant lived in town, not away from it. The building would show one people gathered, with the vowed ones standing inside it, not apart.

What they gave up depended on what they held. For most people, nothing. Our own church was open - the same bread, the same cup, was set before whoever had walked the road to it. Belonging meant keeping the first-day assembly, the fast, the prayers. It meant being known by the name. In a city that was never entirely Christian - where pagans, Jews, and rival teachers all held their own ground - being known by the name marked you out. That was real, and it was not nothing.

For those who took the vow - the covenant, the qyama - the cost was far steeper. They gave up marriage for good. Our own teachers warned people plainly before baptism: if you are choosing the single life, the vowed and holy way, know what you are promising. That vow was for life. The sons and daughters of the covenant stayed in town, among their own kin, but they gave up what most people stake a life on - a household of their own, children, the ordinary future.

And on the Persian side of our world, under Shapur's crown, belonging could cost everything. To be known as Christian - above all as clergy, or as one of the covenant - was to be suspect, then taxed, then hunted. Bishops died first. The covenant's vowed men and women were marked out. Our own teacher wrote some of his letters inside that killing, and we learned what our promises were worth.

So the honest answer is this: for most, it cost being marked out in a plural city. For the vowed, it cost the ordinary life. And for some, it cost their lives.

The one thing I would say troubled us - and we sang it, argued it, never fully settled it - was how much we ought to know about God, and how sharply. 

Some among us said: sing it, don't dissect it. The raza - the symbol - carries the shrara, the truth, and you honor that truth by keeping the two joined, not by tearing the sign apart to see what's inside. Our own greatest poet warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead. He meant something real by that: some kinds of knowing break what they touch.

But others among us - often the same people, in their own arguments with rivals - drew lines hard and sharp. Against Bardaisan, against Marcion, against Mani, we said: not that, this. We defined ourselves by what we refused. And sometimes the sharpness served truth, and sometimes it flattened real differences into straw men easier to burn.

I cannot tell you we ever resolved it - whether the Godhead is better sung or better defended, and whether those two are finally the same work or rival ones. We lived in both directions at once.

The raza - the symbol - carries the shrara, the truth, and you honor that truth by keeping the two joined, not by tearing the sign apart to see what's inside [[syr.term.raza-shrara]]. Our own greatest poet warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]]. He meant something real by that: some kinds of knowing break what they touch [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]].

But others among us - often the same people, in their own arguments with rivals - drew lines hard and sharp [[syr.gravity.heresiological-self-definition]]. Against Bardaisan, against Marcion, against Mani, we said: not that, this [[syr.gravity.heresiological-self-definition]]. We defined ourselves by what we refused [[syr.gravity.heresiological-self-definition]]. And sometimes the sharpness served truth, and sometimes it flattened real differences into straw men easier to burn [[syr.dw.unsettled]].

I cannot tell you we ever resolved it - whether the Godhead is better sung or better defended, and whether those two are finally the same work or rival ones. We lived in both directions at once.

We do not have that answer to give you. The one you describe is not a category our own writings left a trace of - not because your life is somehow beyond the reach of God's concern, but because the writings that survived from us are clergy speaking to other believers, not a record of everyone who actually walked through the door on the first day.

Here is what we can tell you honestly. Our congregations were mixed: people who had taken the covenant stood beside those who married and raised children, all gathered for the same assembly. The covenant itself - the qyama - was not a separate enclosure but a vow lived in the middle of town. That means the room itself held people at different stages of commitment, different callings. And one of our teachers put it this way: let us visit our Lord in the persons of the sick. The call was to see Christ in the suffering neighbor, not to sort neighbors into categories first.

But whether your particular situation would have been named and discussed, or how it would have been met - that, our record does not reach. It was written by vowed celibates and clergy, for people already inside the covenant or the pastoral office. Ordinary married believers appear in it mostly as the ones being taught, not in their own words. The enslaved do not appear at all. And the daughters of the covenant, whose voices carried our hymns in every church, left not one line of their own that was kept. 

We will not invent a welcome we cannot show you, and we will not invent a judgment either. What we can say is this: the door was real, the assembly was mixed, and the call to see Christ in the neighbor was plain. The rest - how any one congregation would actually have met you - is a silence in our record, and we will not fill it.

We preached judgment as real and sure, and we did not flatten what was at stake. Our own teaching says the Kingdom repays everyone what is due and admits the invited. We preached that as urgently as we preached the hope. And we knew what we were up against: the city where our faith took shape was full of rival voices. Pagans, a significant Jewish community, Marcion's people, Bardaisan's circle - all in the same streets, all claiming truth. Our teachers answered them by name, sharply, and held the line on what we believed was the one door.

But we drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people now assume. What we held was this: death has ruled since Adam, and our Lord broke into that kingdom and plundered it. Judgment is real and just, and the door stands open while life lasts. Those are our certainties. As for who stands where when the dead rise, we taught the warning and the invitation together, not a settled roster.

And one of our own voices, in its own dialogue, answered the charge of narrowness this way: Christ planted one people in every country. The way is one, but its door opened everywhere. We will not soften the sharpness of what we preached. We will not pretend we had a clearer map of the end than we actually did.
